title: Coral Reefs Face Collapse in Next 50 Years, Say Experts
paragraphs: Coral reefs support a quarter of all marine species, provide food and income for coastal communities, and help protect shorelines from storms.
But nearly all of the world's shallow-water coral reef ecosystems face a high risk of collapse by 2075, mainly because of warming oceans and heat waves.

That's the warning from a new assessment by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). It examined reefs across 127 tropical and subtropical regions and classified 96% of these ecosystems as critically endangered — its highest threat category.
These include Australia's Great Barrier Reef and the Red Sea's coral reefs. The findings reflect both damage already observed and the effects of projected ocean warming.
So how does warmer water threaten these underwater communities?

When water gets too warm, corals can lose the tiny algae living in their tissues that provide much of their food. That makes them turn white, a process called bleaching. Corals can recover, but prolonged heat stress can kill them.
As heat waves become more frequent, reefs may have less time to recover before the next one strikes.

When a reef ecosystem collapses, its hard corals largely disappear, leaving algae, rubble and sponges in their place. The reef can no longer support the rich variety of marine life that once depended on it.
However, being critically endangered doesn't mean a reef has already collapsed. Most still have living coral, and researchers say there is still time to help them recover.
"The risk of coral reef collapse is escalating, but this must be a wake-up call rather than a cause for despair," said Mishal Gudka, the assessment's scientific lead.

Cutting greenhouse gas emissions is essential to limiting further warming. But local action matters too: reducing pollution and overfishing, protecting reefs and restoring damaged areas can give them a better chance of survival.
